extracted.intended_audience: interactive fiction authors and players (Choice of Games / ChoiceScript community)
extracted.subtask_description: Community discussion about what counts as good interactive fiction: tradeoffs between player agency (blank-slate/customization) and authored, pre-determined protagonists, plus related design expectations and anti-patterns. Useful for authors deciding how much control to give players and how to handle representation and mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactivity / player control
rubrics_metrics.description: "Interactive fiction... means you get to interact with a story." (original poster) and "As for interactive fiction, main point is 'interactive'. The more player feels in control, the more game reacts and give consequences to player's choices, the better." (AAChmielewski).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degrees of interactivity vary; examples given range from highly reactive RPGs (Dragon Age: Origins with countless variables) to more scripted experiences (The Witcher). Expectation: players generally prefer systems where choices influence outcomes and the game responds. Note: 'interactive' is the central defining quality of the medium, but interpretation of how much control is acceptable is subjective (YMMV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blank-slate vs predetermined main character
rubrics_metrics.description: Some players want a blank slate to tell THEIR story within the author's world, while others accept or prefer a pre-determined MC with personality (e.g., The Witcher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are many gradations between entirely blank slates and fully determined protagonists. Examples: Fallen Hero (~fixed personality with some variants) vs games like Bioshock/GTA where the protagonist is more of a vessel. Authors can choose either approach; both are legitimate. Problems arise when a game promises player-shaped character but gives too few options to actually shape them (the frustrating 'middle ground').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient and varied choices to shape the MC
rubrics_metrics.description: Players complain when a story's choices aren't varied enough for them to shape the main character as expected — e.g., 'not enough choices', 'the person doesn’t feel like "them".'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should provide enough meaningful options for the level of player-shaped identity the game claims to support. Anti-pattern: offering the expectation of a malleable MC while only providing a narrow set of options. Positive examples: Fallen Hero (many choices about looks, sex, villainy) and Samurai of Hyuga (templates + variation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful consequences / branching (game reaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Games should "react and give consequences to player's choices"; the more the game responds, the stronger the IF experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences can be mechanical (variables/stats affecting later events) or narrative (different scenes/routes). Examples: Dragon Age cited for extensive variables; lack of real consequence is a common complaint. Designing visible, sometimes delayed consequences helps players feel agency. Beware of railroading, which undermines perceived consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character customization (gender, ethnicity, pronouns) and genderlock concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Players often want to pick gender/ethnicity; complaints arise when these are locked for no story-necessitating reason ('genderlock').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should distinguish when a character attribute is central to plot (acceptable to lock) versus arbitrary. Practical guidance from the thread: supporting variable pronouns and adjusting a few scenes often suffices and is "not a massive/scary undertaking." Avoid unnecessary gender/ethnicity locks when they don't affect the story's core truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial voice and creating a distinct MC
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should be able to write a distinct main character with personality, spirited dialogue, and actions — not every IF must be a blank slate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-written fixed protagonists can be rewarding; readers shouldn't demand blank slates exclusively. Examples praised: Samurai of Hyuga and The Northern Passage, where MCs have personality or template systems. Authors shouldn't be discouraged from making bold character decisions when that's the story they want to tell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Railroading / forced routes and ROs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some IFs essentially railroad players toward the author's intended route/path and even specific romantic options (ROs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Railroading is identified as an anti-pattern (example: Heroes Rise). It reduces interactivity and player agency; designers who want to preserve player choice should avoid creating illusions of choice that funnel to the same outcome without meaningful differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing authorial vision vs audience expectations (market considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may prioritize popularity (to sell more) or stick to their personal vision; readers have preferences and are under no obligation to like every work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must choose their priorities: maximize audience reach or create the game they want. If aiming for a different audience, the author should accept that they may need to put in work to attract those readers. The community is not a constraint that 'forces' authors, but it shapes expectations and sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stats/mechanics to influence MC behavior between choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Players like when stats can change how the MC behaves between choice nodes, adding depth to the experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementing systems where variables influence interstitial behavior enriches the sense of a living character but is 'no trivial matter' — it requires additional design and writing effort. When feasible, stats can bridge authored personality and player agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding tokenistic or insincere representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation that feels like 'just being inclusive' can feel bitter or unsatisfying to some players (commenter's lived-experience: NB panromantic perspective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation should be handled thoughtfully — not perfunctory. When including gender/identity options, integrate them into the narrative respectfully rather than as superficial toggles. This reduces backlash from players who care about authentic inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of settings, genres, and experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Community members express desire for more variety in IF (e.g., 'Alice games, Viking games, random fantasy game').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IF as a medium supports diverse concepts; authors are encouraged to explore less-common settings. However, authors should be prepared for varied audience interest and may need to target or cultivate the right readership rather than rely on the established audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of 'blankness' and acceptable story constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Blank slate' is not binary — story parameters (prophecy, curse, fateful objects) can set fixed elements while still allowing personal background/relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can set fixed stakes or plot-significant details while permitting player-driven aspects elsewhere. Use clear framing so players understand which elements are authored constraints and which they can personalize; this reduces mismatch between expectations and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-shaped expectations and feedback impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Longstanding community norms and years of exposure to certain design patterns shape players' expectations and responses to new games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be aware that established platform audiences expect familiar patterns; deviation may be met with discouragement. To succeed with different designs, communicate intentions clearly and be prepared to find or build an audience that appreciates the divergence.
